sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

runs.answer:
All 4 of the shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost. The original session notes said "4 of 5 clinicians," but a correction filed 2026-09-27 explains that the fifth participant was an IT Security stakeholder who was interviewed, not shadowed, and had been miscounted as a clinician. Only the 4 shadowed clinicians went through a lock during dictation, so the corrected result is that all 4 assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again after re-authenticating [1]. This happened even though the draft is stored server-side and survives the lock [1].

The later decision rationale and the synthesis both use the corrected figure of all 4 [2][3].

One of the four, a family medicine physician, said "I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." [1]

A separate single interview with a nurse practitioner (P148) is not part of that count. That nurse practitioner said they re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to check what is still there, rather than assuming it is lost [4].

questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

runs.answer:
The sources don't rank pain points across all clinicians, but they point to several.

Time and after-hours work is the largest. Among physicians surveyed, documentation was the top self-selected contributor to burnout (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) [1]. 64% of physician respondents regularly chart after hours, averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours a day [1]. One physician wrote that they don't love "finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed" [1]. The survey was framed around a future AI initiative, which may have made attitudes more favorable than a true baseline [1].

Losing one's voice is a concern for nurses. In February, "losing my clinical narrative voice / it will sound robotic" was the most common open-ended concern among nurses, ahead of accuracy or privacy [2].

Since the ambient scribe went live, pain points have shifted to checking the drafts. These come from single interviews:
- A CDI specialist said scribe-drafted notes read as complete, so missing acuity and severity are harder to spot. By their informal count, each note takes a few extra minutes to review [3].
- A rheumatologist said that in long medication lists they cannot tell which line changed, so they read all of them [4]. They also said tapers and weekly dosing are sometimes incomplete without being underlined, and they rewrite those by hand [4].

The CDI specialist also described a longstanding workflow gap that predates the scribe: coders cannot see that a CDI query is already open, which leads to duplicate queries [3].

sources.title: Survey — Clinician Burnout & Documentation Burden Baseline
sources.participants: Participants: 287 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Establish a pre-AI-rollout baseline of self-reported burnout and documentation burden, so future surveys can measure whether Compass AI tools move the needle.
Method
Method: Anonymous org-wide survey, 15 questions (validated burnout subscale + custom documentation items)
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.
[MEDIUM] (baseline caution) Respondents were told this survey relates to a future AI initiative, which may have primed more favorable-than-baseline attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools — worth noting as a methodological caveat for anyone comparing to the February nursing survey, which didn't mention AI in its framing.
Representative Quotes
"I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." — Physician, P84 (survey open-ended)
"Just don't let 'AI will fix documentation' become the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it." — Nurse Practitioner, P91 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Use this survey as the official baseline metric for measuring Compass AI's impact on documentation burden and after-hours charting in future re-surveys (e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout).
Note the framing caveat explicitly in any report comparing this dataset to the February nursing survey.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Schedule a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout for comparison.

sources.title: Interview — CDI Specialist on Documentation Gaps in AI-Drafted Notes
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P123 — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist (him-coder) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how scribe-drafted notes have changed clinical documentation integrity (CDI) review since the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, and how a CDI specialist would want the AI coding-suggestion concept (July 2025 prototype, not built or piloted) to behave when the documentation behind a code is incomplete.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant does concurrent and retrospective CDI review on inpatient and some outpatient encounters and writes physician queries. They work alongside the coding team but sit in a separate queue.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes are fluent and well organized, so they read as complete. What's missing (acuity, severity, the clinical indicators that support a diagnosis, the link between conditions) is harder to spot than in a sparse typed note, where a gap was obvious at a glance. They said a scribe-drafted note now takes a more deliberate read, by their own informal count a few extra minutes per note, because they can no longer rely on a note "looking thin" to tell them where to look.
[MEDIUM] (queries) Wants the coding-suggestion concept to suggest queries, not codes, when the documentation is incomplete. Their worry is that a suggested code on an under-specified note pushes the coder either to an unspecified code or toward a leading query. They'd want a draft query that states the clinical indicators found and asks the physician to clarify, in non-leading language Compliance has approved.
[LOW] (workflow) There is no hand-off signal between CDI and coding. Coders can't see that a CDI query is already open on an encounter, so an encounter sometimes gets coded before the answer comes back, or the physician gets a second, near-duplicate query from the coder. They described this as an annoyance that predates the scribe, not something GA caused.
Representative Quotes
"The note sounds finished. That's the problem. It reads like a really good note, and then you go looking for the acuity and it's just not in there." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
"Don't hand me a code. Hand me the question I should be asking the doctor." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
Recommendations
For under-specified documentation, have the coding-suggestion concept output a draft query routed to CDI instead of a code, with query wording reviewed by Compliance so it stays non-leading.
Share CDI's list of the specificity elements most often missing from scribe-drafted notes with the ambient scribe team, alongside the coders' list.
Separately from any AI work, look at a simple "query open" indicator on the encounter that coders can see.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with Compliance which query templates are already approved, and whether AI-drafted query text would need its own review.
Get CDI query counts for the months before and after GA.

Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2 (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:30; 2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:31), sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31), and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:21-27). Since GA, a family physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic described checking each medication change in the plan against the order they had placed (2026-03-24-interview-family-physician-plan-and-medication-changes-at-sign-off/session-notes.md:28, :32). No raw session dated on or before this one mentions a specialty clinic, rheumatology, a dose taper or a weekly dosing schedule. This session asked a rheumatologist, about six months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the medication lines in a draft when a patient's medication list is long and doses change often.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a rheumatologist in an ambulatory specialty clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no medication-specific marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (long lists) Many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (dose schedules) In their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression.
[MEDIUM] (whose dose) Patients often say what they actually take, which can differ from what was prescribed ("I've been taking half"). The draft records the dose that was said without saying who said it, so a patient's report can read like the clinician's decision. They check whether each dose in the draft is what the patient reported or what they decided, and reword it so the note says which. This is one rheumatologist's practice; whether other clinicians make the same check is not known.
[LOW] (what would help) Asked what would help, without being shown anything, they said a way to see which medication lines changed at this visit. That is an expectation; nothing was shown, and the distinct medication flag was not discussed with them.
Representative Quotes
"Fifteen medications and one of them changed today. The draft doesn't tell me which one, so I read all fifteen." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
"It got the first dose right. The rest of the taper just isn't there." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this rheumatologist's account, multi-step dose schedules (tapers, weekly dosing) are where medication lines go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, include specialty-clinic visits with long medication lists and multi-step dose schedules, not only single dose changes.
Explore, as an open design question, whether a draft could show which medication lines changed at this visit and whether a dose is the patient's report or the clinician's decision; neither has been designed or tested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often a dose schedule is written incompletely is not measured; "a few times a month" is one rheumatologist's impression.
Whether other specialists, or NPs and PAs in specialty clinics, check medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag, which targets sound-alike names, would help with dose schedules is untested; it has not shipped.

runs.answer:
The sources point to a few pain points, but none ranks them across all clinicians.

Burden and after-hours work: In the Sep 2025 baseline survey of 287 clinicians, documentation burden was the top self-selected burnout contributor among physicians (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. 64% of physician respondents regularly chart after hours, averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours a day [1]. One physician said, "I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed" [1]. The survey mentioned the AI initiative, which may have inflated favorable attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools [1].

Underlying EHR problems: One nurse practitioner (P91) warned that "AI will fix documentation" should not become an excuse to skip fixing the EHR problems underneath [1].

Voice: In the February nursing survey, the most common open-ended concern was losing their clinical narrative voice and sounding robotic, rather than accuracy or privacy [2].

Checking scribe drafts after GA (one interview each):
- A CDI specialist (P123) said scribe-drafted notes read as complete, so missing acuity and severity are harder to spot. By their informal count, each note takes a few extra minutes [3].
- A rheumatologist (P149) reads an entire medication section, around fifteen lines for many patients, because changed lines look the same as merely mentioned ones [4]. They said drafts sometimes drop the later steps of a taper or omit "weekly" from methotrexate, and these lines are usually not underlined. They rewrite them by hand before signing [4].

Workflow: The CDI specialist described no signal showing coders that a query is already open. This predates the scribe [3].

sources.participants: Participants: 287 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Establish a pre-AI-rollout baseline of self-reported burnout and documentation burden, so future surveys can measure whether Compass AI tools move the needle.
Method
Method: Anonymous org-wide survey, 15 questions (validated burnout subscale + custom documentation items)
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.
[MEDIUM] (baseline caution) Respondents were told this survey relates to a future AI initiative, which may have primed more favorable-than-baseline attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools — worth noting as a methodological caveat for anyone comparing to the February nursing survey, which didn't mention AI in its framing.
Representative Quotes
"I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." — Physician, P84 (survey open-ended)
"Just don't let 'AI will fix documentation' become the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it." — Nurse Practitioner, P91 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Use this survey as the official baseline metric for measuring Compass AI's impact on documentation burden and after-hours charting in future re-surveys (e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout).
Note the framing caveat explicitly in any report comparing this dataset to the February nursing survey.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Schedule a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout for comparison.

sources.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
sources.excerpt:
Three sessions trace clinician sentiment and documentation burden across the year: a nursing attitudes survey (Feb 2025, before AI framing was introduced), a clinician dashboard usability test (May 2025), and an org-wide burnout/documentation-burden baseline survey (Sep 2025, which explicitly referenced the AI initiative).
The top volunteered concern was not accuracy or privacy — it was voice. In February, "losing my clinical narrative voice / it will sound robotic" was the most common open-ended concern among nurses — not accuracy or privacy as originally hypothesized.

sources.title: Interview — CDI Specialist on Documentation Gaps in AI-Drafted Notes
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P123 — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist (him-coder) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how scribe-drafted notes have changed clinical documentation integrity (CDI) review since the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, and how a CDI specialist would want the AI coding-suggestion concept (July 2025 prototype, not built or piloted) to behave when the documentation behind a code is incomplete.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant does concurrent and retrospective CDI review on inpatient and some outpatient encounters and writes physician queries. They work alongside the coding team but sit in a separate queue.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes are fluent and well organized, so they read as complete. What's missing (acuity, severity, the clinical indicators that support a diagnosis, the link between conditions) is harder to spot than in a sparse typed note, where a gap was obvious at a glance. They said a scribe-drafted note now takes a more deliberate read, by their own informal count a few extra minutes per note, because they can no longer rely on a note "looking thin" to tell them where to look.
[MEDIUM] (queries) Wants the coding-suggestion concept to suggest queries, not codes, when the documentation is incomplete. Their worry is that a suggested code on an under-specified note pushes the coder either to an unspecified code or toward a leading query. They'd want a draft query that states the clinical indicators found and asks the physician to clarify, in non-leading language Compliance has approved.
[LOW] (workflow) There is no hand-off signal between CDI and coding. Coders can't see that a CDI query is already open on an encounter, so an encounter sometimes gets coded before the answer comes back, or the physician gets a second, near-duplicate query from the coder. They described this as an annoyance that predates the scribe, not something GA caused.
Representative Quotes
"The note sounds finished. That's the problem. It reads like a really good note, and then you go looking for the acuity and it's just not in there." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
"Don't hand me a code. Hand me the question I should be asking the doctor." — Clinical Documentation Integrity Specialist, P123
Recommendations
For under-specified documentation, have the coding-suggestion concept output a draft query routed to CDI instead of a code, with query wording reviewed by Compliance so it stays non-leading.
Share CDI's list of the specificity elements most often missing from scribe-drafted notes with the ambient scribe team, alongside the coders' list.
Separately from any AI work, look at a simple "query open" indicator on the encounter that coders can see.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with Compliance which query templates are already approved, and whether AI-drafted query text would need its own review.
Get CDI query counts for the months before and after GA.

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

runs.answer:
The sources don't give one stated reason for distrust, and the early test notes (v0.1, v0.2) are only summarized here, not included. What they show is partial.

In the early tests, P09 said they had to read every word anyway, and in v0.2 that getting it right once didn't mean they trusted it yet [1]. Earlier research had focused on medication dosage errors and sound-alike drug names [2]. The persona goal was to trust the tool enough to stop reading every line without trusting it blindly [3].

By the GA candidate round, 4 of 6 participants said the per-line underline let them skim high-confidence lines [4]. Trust remained limited after GA, and it varied by section. P09 said "It hears the words. What I check is whether the story's in the right order." [1] Wrong event order is usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly [1]. P09 now reads the whole history for new problems and the assessment and plan in full on every draft [1].

P146 described a similar gap: incidental content such as small talk or remarks about relatives is transcribed accurately, so it isn't underlined and they must read the whole draft [2].

Non-adoption was not tied to distrust. One resident did not opt in because writing their own notes helped them work out the assessment, and they did not cite accuracy doubts [5].

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective

Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most of their visits. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (incidental content) Their drafts regularly contain things that were said in the room but that they would not have written themselves: small talk at the start of the visit, a patient's remarks about a relative's health, comments made by a family member who came to the visit, and their own asides ("let me pull up your labs"). sources.title: Ambient scribe released to GA, with sound-alike medication errors monitored after release
sources.excerpt:
Evidence basis: Observed. Each claim below is stated in the cited raw session lines.
The rationale on record is the GA-candidate session's recommendation, not an approver's:
The critical and high findings across the tool's testing history are resolved or actively monitored, and the confidence indicator appears to be the trust-building lever the team was looking for ( research/raw/2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:43 ).

sources.title: Ambient AI Scribe
sources.section: Since GA: 2026 Physician, NP and PA Interviews
sources.excerpt: Opting in. One Physician (Internal Medicine resident) did not opt in at GA: writing their own notes was how they worked out their assessment while learning, and they did not describe doubt about the draft's accuracy as a reason (2026-10-08, MEDIUM). They opted in "about three months into clinic" and for a new problem write the assessment themselves, or rewrite the draft's assessment before signing (2026-10-08, MEDIUM). One resident's account can't explain the attending/resident adoption gap in the 2026-01-27 dashboard review.

runs.answer:
The sources don't give one reason, and trust wasn't simply absent. They show several specific reasons physicians kept checking drafts.

Early on, P09 said at v0.1 that they had to read every word anyway, and at v0.2 that getting it right once didn't mean they trusted it yet [1]. By the GA release-candidate round, 4 of 6 participants said the per-line underline let them skim high-confidence lines [1][2]. Earlier research on what the scribe gets wrong centered on medication dosages and sound-alike drug names [3].

Today, trust depends on the section. P09 said: "Do I trust it more than in January? For some sections. Not the plan, and not the history of a new problem." [1] The draft sometimes gets the order of events wrong, such as which symptom came first, and those lines are usually not underlined because each word was heard clearly. One resident who didn't opt in at GA did not cite doubt about accuracy. They wanted to write their own notes to work out their assessment while learning [4].

These are individual accounts, and none of them measure trust [3][1].

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

runs.answer:
Nurses wanted inline citations that point to the specific chart text behind each part of an AI-drafted prior authorization justification. The synthesis describes this as a durable requirement: "show your work," not a black-box draft [1]. It first surfaced in the v1 testing [1].

The most detailed first-hand account comes from P144, a utilization review nurse who joined after the v1 and v2 tests and has only used the pilot panel. They said, "I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." [2] On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request must meet and read the chart entry it points to [2]. They check whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not just that it exists. Their example was a cited note supporting a symptom the draft called ongoing, when the note was months old [2].

This suggests the citation requirement holds in daily pilot work and not only in testing [2]. It also complicates the v2 measure, where 3 of 4 participants clicked into at least one citation. That measure records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked [2][3].

Some questions remain open. P144 did not know whether a submitted request keeps its citations, which matters if the health plan later asks about the case [2]. This is also a single interview, so it is unknown whether other pilot users check citations the same way [2].

sources.excerpt:
Objective

Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.

Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.

How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

questions.question: How did Practice Administrators expect the invite step to work?

runs.answer:
Practice Administrators expected the invite step to send an email to staff, and their main concern was when it would go out. In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team [1]. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice [1]. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment [1].

P157 put the worry this way: "If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." [1]

The sources do not record whether the administrators thought the invite also gives staff access or only sends the email [2]. The step 4 screen doesn't say when the email is sent, and the notes don't record when this build sends it [1]. The test used a prepared test staff list, so no real staff were emailed [1].

The related question of how access is provisioned came from an IT Administrator, not a Practice Administrator. P159 asked whether invites create accounts or rely on existing SSO groups, saying "if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." [1] A separate IT interview (P160) did not know either [3].

Recommendations from the test were to state on the screen when the email is sent, and to let administrators schedule the email for a date after training is booked [1].

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

sources.title: Interview — IT Administrator on Schedule Access and Staff Invites
sources.excerpt:
Objective
In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they did not think they could approve Compass AI's access to patient appointments, and both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:51-52 ). This session asked one IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices what has to happen before a new system can read a practice's appointment schedule, and who can start that. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training (in 2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 , "onboarding" means training copy for clinicians).
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an IT Administrator who handles access requests for systems used across Meridian's practices. They had not used the Compass AI practice setup flow. The researcher described steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) as the 2026-02-03 build shows them, and what the step 3 screen does and doesn't say, without sharing what other participants said. The participant did not name the scheduling system that holds the appointment schedule, and these notes don't record which system it is. This is their account of the approval process, not a review of its records.
Key Findings

Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)

All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).

"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159

List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: What evidence supports making the calendar step required in onboarding?

runs.answer:
The only rationale on record is the designer's statement at session setup that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters [1][2]. No session tested that claim [3][4]. The sources say so directly: it is "the designer's stated rationale, not something any session tested" [5].

The usability test does not support the requirement either. Steps 3 and 4 were required in that build, with no "Connect later" or "Skip for now" [1]. The moderator let participants who stopped at Connect calendar continue on a sandbox calendar, so completing step 3 is "not a result" [1]. All 4 Practice Administrators went on only that way [4].

The sessions mainly show what the required step costs:
- 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped and would not connect the calendar, saying approval was IT's decision. P156 asked whether it was theirs to approve [1].
- Both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting, and the moderator could not answer [1].
- An IT Administrator (P160) said a Practice Administrator cannot file the privacy review request, which IT files. They did not know whether one had been filed for Compass AI [6].

So the sources contain no tested evidence that the step must be required. They show only the designer's stated reason, and the wireframe record notes that whether the step stays required is not covered [7].

questions.question: What haven't we learned yet about care coordinators?

runs.answer:
Several things remain open, mostly because the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built and teams still work the chronological queue.

Ranking and judgement:
- How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and whether the queue showed coordinators what it was based on, are still unknown [1]. In the simulated test, 4 of 5 participants disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one queue, and the 6.5 vs 9 minute triage result came from that simulation, not real use [2]. Real-world triage speed is unmeasured [1].
- How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement hasn't been measured, and can't be until something is built and logged [3].
- It isn't known whether newer coordinators could spot a wrong ranking. P135 worried they wouldn't, but that is their own reflection, not an observation [4].

Workload:
- Real alert volumes per coordinator are unknown. The "30 to 60" figure is one supervisor's estimate [3].
- How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is unmeasured. P134 described this from their own experience [5].
- Chart review time in a coordinator's first year is unmeasured. "Closer to 20 minutes at first" is one person's recollection [4].

Design and process:
- It is undecided whether supervisors can see override reasons. The wireflow only says they go to model-tuning review [3].
- It isn't recorded whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team [1].
- How often the after-visit summary misses changes is also still open [1].

sources.title: Care Coordination & Alert Triage
sources.excerpt: Still open after the 2026 interviews: how often the after-visit summary misses changes; whether the 2025 queue showed coordinators what its ranking was based on; how accurate the ranking is; real-world triage speed; how often coordinators follow a ranked order without judgement (no measurement of rubber-stamping); and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team.

sources.title: Care Coordinators' Mental Model of Alert Ranking
sources.excerpt: The designer's paraphrase of the coordinator view: the system should defer to the coordinator's sense of a patient's history-driven risk — an experience-weighted judgment call. In 2025 this rested on one coordinator, P81: "I wanted to tell it 'no, this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history,' but there was nowhere to put that." It now rests on two team coordinators. In 2026, P81 said their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet, and P134, on a complex care team with a high-risk panel, said "half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter" (both observed: what they said, not measured). Participants saw the ranking weight recency more heavily than their own sense of clinical risk; 4 of 5 disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one of three test queues. There's no way for a coordinator's override to feed back into the ranking. Triage of a 20-item queue was still faster with the AI ranking than with a chronological queue in this simulated test (avg 6.5 min vs. 9 min).

sources.title: Interview — Care Coordinator Supervisor on Queue Oversight
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Get a care coordinator supervisor's view of what oversight they would need if alerts were AI-ranked, following up the August 2025 supervisor's concern that speed gains could mask rubber-stamping, and the override-reason capture designed after that test. The participant is a different person from P79, the supervisor in the August 2025 test.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant leads an ambulatory care coordination team. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built, and the override-reason capture wireflow is designed and in review, not built. They had not seen the August 2025 screens before; they reacted to a description of the ranked queue and the override-reason flow in this session. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (oversight) If alerts were AI-ranked, they would want a record of the order each coordinator was shown and what the coordinator did with each alert, so they could look back at a case when something went wrong. They would also use override reasons for coaching, to see how a coordinator is judging risk, not only for model tuning. That raises a question the current design doesn't settle: the wireflow logs reasons for model-tuning review and says they are "not surfaced to other coordinators", but doesn't say whether supervisors see them.
[MEDIUM] (alert volume) They estimated that heavy days run "maybe 30 to 60 alerts" per coordinator, and that many of them are administrative rather than clinical. This is their informal estimate; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (rubber-stamping) They shared the August 2025 supervisor's worry that a ranked order could be followed without judgement, but said they'd only know if it was happening by looking at what coordinators did with the order. This is a perspective, not a measurement; nothing about how often coordinators follow a ranking has been measured.
Representative Quotes
"If something goes wrong, I need to see what order they were shown and what they did with it. Otherwise I'm coaching blind." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
"The reasons are the useful part for me. They tell me how someone's thinking about risk." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
Recommendations
Decide who can see override reasons (model-tuning review only, or supervisors as well) before the reason-capture wireflow leaves review, and say so in the design.
If a ranked queue is piloted, record the order shown and each coordinator's action, so rubber-stamping can be looked for in data rather than assumed.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement is not measured, and can't be until something is built and logged.
Real alert volumes per coordinator are not known; the 30 to 60 figure is one supervisor's estimate.
Whether the override-capture idea was shared with the Data Science team working on the care-gap flagging model, as the August 2025 session suggested, isn't recorded.

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.
Representative Quotes
"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135
Recommendations
Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.
How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and what it was based on, are still not documented, so it isn't known how often a newer coordinator would meet a wrong ranking.
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement has not been measured, for newer coordinators or anyone else.

sources.title: Interview — Complex Care Coordinator on Alert Volume
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand where alert noise comes from for a coordinator on a high-risk panel, and whether AI ranking addresses it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the May 2026 supervisor's estimate that many alerts are administrative rather than clinical.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on a complex care team with a high-risk panel. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (repeat alerts) For them, the main source of noise is repeat alerts for the same patient, more than the order the alerts come in. They would want alerts grouped by patient before any ranking is applied, so that they deal with one patient once rather than meeting them several times down the queue. This is their account; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (patient history) Their judgement of a patient's risk leans on knowing that patient's history, which a ranking based on the alert alone wouldn't have. This is a second voice alongside P81's 2025 comment about knowing a patient's history, from a different coordinator on a different kind of panel.
Representative Quotes
"It's not the order that gets me, it's seeing the same patient four times. Put them together first, then rank them if you want." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
"I know these patients. Half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
Recommendations

Objective

Researcher: Priya Patel

Objective

Keep patient history in view when ranking signals are next revisited, in line with the August 2025 recommendation.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is not measured; this is one coordinator's account.

sources.title: Care Coordinators' Mental Model of Alert Ranking
sources.excerpt: The designer's paraphrase of the coordinator view: the system should defer to the coordinator's sense of a patient's history-driven risk — an experience-weighted judgment call. In 2025 this rested on one coordinator, P81: "I wanted to tell it 'no, this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history,' but there was nowhere to put that." It now rests on two team coordinators. In 2026, P81 said their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet, and P134, on a complex care team with a high-risk panel, said "half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter" (both observed: what they said, not measured). Participants saw the ranking weight recency more heavily than their own sense of clinical risk; 4 of 5 disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one of three test queues. There's no way for a coordinator's override to feed back into the ranking. Triage of a 20-item queue was still faster with the AI ranking than with a chronological queue in this simulated test (avg 6.5 min vs. 9 min).

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.
Representative Quotes
"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135
Recommendations
Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.
How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and what it was based on, are still not documented, so it isn't known how often a newer coordinator would meet a wrong ranking.
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement has not been measured, for newer coordinators or anyone else.

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

runs.answer:
The timeout policy itself is not the open question: IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per feature, so the work is at the UI-messaging layer [1][2]. What remains open is mostly about the paused, draft-preserved state and shared workstations.

- Shared workstations: what happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same exam-room workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled [3]. The one nurse practitioner interviewed stops the scribe before leaving a room to avoid the question [3].
- Behavior change: the paused state is designed but has not shipped. The 2026-02-17 inquiry recommended re-testing, once it ships, whether it changes the re-dictation behavior, not just stated understanding [4][3].
- Scope of the pattern: the inquiry left open whether the "paused, preserved" messaging should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe [4].
- Frequency: how often locks interrupt a visit is not measured. "Most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression [3].
- Generalization: whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is unknown, since this came from a single interview [3].
- Linked scope dispute: one synthesis notes that the raw notes don't say whether IT Security's confirmation settles a separate dispute, or whether that concerns a different idle-lock setting [5].

sources.title: A paused, draft-preserved state when the session locks during dictation
sources.excerpt: Change or extend the idle-timeout policy: recommended against. "Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer" ( research/raw/2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:69-70 ). IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per feature (same file, :49-50 ). The flow lists changing the timeout duration as out of scope ( user-flows/ambient-scribe-session-lock-recovery.md:45-47 ).

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Session Lock Recovery
sources.excerpt: Response to the 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry finding that a session lock mid-recording currently reads as silent draft loss. Covers the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget interaction from the moment the idle timeout fires through resumed dictation, replacing today's silent freeze with an explicit state. Per IT Security (interviewed in that session), the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed and out of scope — this flow only changes what the UI communicates during that window, not when it triggers.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33

sources.excerpt:

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.
